title: Area VII review: Navigation Aids
intro: These questions mix the two Tasks of Area VII: intercepting and tracking VOR, NDB, DME and GPS courses and DME arcs, and holding procedures. Most put both in one flight the way your learner will meet them: an arc that ends at a holding fix, a radial tracked to a VOR hold, a DME hold after an outbound radial, an arc to a localizer with a missed approach hold, a GPS standing in for a failed DME or a missing ADF, a hold in lieu of procedure turn at the end of a NoPT arc, and a radio failure while holding.

questions.q: Using Figure 9-17, your learner tracks inbound on the OKT 325° radial at 120 knots groundspeed to join the 10 DME arc. ATC has given her advance notice that she will hold at the OKT 10 DME fix on the 045 radial, farther along the arc. What plan do you want to hear?
options: Turn onto the arc at 10.0 DME, the arc distance, and slow to holding speed as she crosses the fix
Turn onto the arc at 10.5 DME, and be at or below holding speed at least 3 minutes before the fix
Turn onto the arc at 9.5 DME, the charted lead point, and slow to holding speed on the first outbound leg
Turn onto the arc at 11.0 DME for a full 1 NM lead, and slow to holding speed 1 minute before the fix
questions.why: At 150 knots groundspeed or less a 0.5 NM lead is satisfactory, so inbound to the 10 DME arc she starts the turn at 10.5 DME; a proportionately greater lead is only for higher groundspeeds [[23:260|IFH 9-17]]. The 9.5 NM lead point in the figure is for joining the arc outbound from the station [[23:261|IFH 9-18]], and turning at 10.0 gives no lead at all. With advance notice of holding, the AIM has her at or below the maximum holding speed at least 3 minutes before crossing the fix [[33:390|AIM 5-3-8j8(a)]], because the speed reduction keeps the airplane from overshooting the holding airspace [[23:302|IFH 10-11]]. Slowing at the fix, or after it, is too late.

questions.q: Your learner's DME receiver has failed. ATC clears her via the 12 DME arc of a VORTAC to the 12 DME fix on the 090 radial, to hold east of that fix with 4-mile legs. Her airplane has an IFR-approved GPS with a current database that includes the VORTAC. What do you teach?
options: Make the VORTAC the active waypoint, fly the arc on GPS distance, and end each outbound leg at 16 miles
Fly the arc on GPS distance, but refuse the hold, because only a working DME may define a DME holding fix
Make the 12 DME fix the active waypoint, and add half a mile to every GPS distance to allow for slant range
Make any waypoint on the 090 radial active, since GPS distance from any point on it gives the same arc
questions.why: A suitable RNAV system, such as IFR-approved GPS, may substitute for a DME that is not operational [[33:116|AIM 1-2-3a]], and may be used to fly an arc based upon DME and to hold over a DME fix [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3c]]. The IFH steps make the DME facility on which the arc is based the active waypoint, the only acceptable one, and keep the arc by GPS distance instead of a DME readout [[23:270|IFH 9-27]]. The hold is east of the fix, so the inbound course runs toward the NAVAID and the outbound leg ends at 12 + 4 = 16 [[33:387|AIM 5-3-8j5]]. GPS distance is horizontal, not slant range, but when it is used solely for DME substitution the difference is negligible and no pilot action is required [[33:388|AIM 5-3-8j6]], so adding a correction is wrong. If the DME fails in flight, she also reports the malfunction to ATC as soon as practical [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(a)]].

questions.q: ATC has told your learner to hold on the 090 radial of a VORTAC ahead. Tuned to it, he hears a single identifier about every 30 seconds and nothing more. His airplane has a VOR receiver and a DME but no GPS. What do you teach?
options: The VOR works but the DME is off, so he can still hold on the radial, using timing in place of distance
Both work; the DME identifier is simply sent less often, so he holds as cleared and keeps listening to it
The facility is in maintenance, so its signals stay usable with care; he holds as cleared and reports it later
The DME works but the VOR is off, so he has no radial to hold on; he tells ATC now and asks for a new clearance
questions.why: The DME identifier is heard once for every three or four VOR identifiers; if only one identifier is heard about every 30 seconds, the DME is working but the associated VOR is not [[23:260|IFH 9-17]] [[33:73|AIM 1-1-7f]]. The tempting answer has that backward. With no VOR he cannot fly the holding radial, and pilots must notify ATC immediately if their radio equipment cannot receive the signals they need to comply with the clearance [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]], and a pilot who meets a navigation problem should change to another source and request an amended clearance as necessary [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13c]]. A facility in maintenance is a warning that it may be unreliable even when signals are received [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]], so that does not make it usable either.

questions.q: Your learner is tracking to a VOR in mountainous terrain, where she will hold. Several minutes before her ETA the CDI briefly swings as it does near the station, and she starts the entry turn. What do you teach?
options: She is in the zone of confusion, so the turn is correct; she should also start the outbound clock now
The swing is propeller modulation; she changes RPM and starts the entry turn once the needle goes still
Some mountain VORs give a brief swing like station approach; she turns at the first complete TO/FROM reversal
The swing shows she passed the station to one side; she turns now and reports the fix to ATC at once
questions.why: At a few stations, usually in mountainous terrain, a brief needle oscillation can look like approaching the station, and pilots should use the TO/FROM indicator to determine positive station passage [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3e]]. When holding at a VOR, the turn outbound begins at the first complete reversal of the TO/FROM indicator [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8g]]. The zone of confusion is the space directly above the station [[23:257|IFH 9-14]], not several minutes out. Some propeller RPM settings can make the CDI fluctuate [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3e]], but the cue to turn is still the TO/FROM reversal, not a steady needle.

questions.q: Your learner's airplane has one VOR/LOC receiver. Her approach starts with a 15 DME arc of a VOR, joins the localizer at a charted lead radial, and the missed approach is a climb to hold at that same VOR. What NAVAID plan do you want in her briefing?
options: VOR for the arc; localizer set at the lead radial and identified before use; VOR retuned and identified for the hold
VOR for the arc; localizer set once its needle starts to center; VOR retuned for the hold, as it was identified before
Localizer set and identified before the arc, with the DME alone giving both the lead radial and the missed approach hold
VOR kept tuned for the arc and the hold, with the GPS flying the localizer course so that no frequency change is needed
questions.why: With a single VOR/LOC receiver, the IFH has the pilot set it to the localizer frequency at the depicted lead radial and use a half-standard-rate turn until the localizer needle starts to move [[23:262|IFH 9-19]]; a needle can't start to center until the receiver is switched. The IPH warns that an arc used as the transition to an ILS means changing NAVAIDs, that planning each change prevents using the wrong one when workload is high, that the primary NAVAID must be positively identified before it is used for course guidance, and that the briefing may need to cover the missed approach NAVAID too [[29:157|IPH 4-17]]. So the VOR is identified again when it is retuned for the hold: listen to the identifier before relying on it [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]. An RNAV system may not provide lateral guidance on a localizer course without reference to raw localizer data [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3c]].

questions.q: On a DME arc your learner keeps the airplane symbol on the magenta arc and ignores the DME. Then she lets the GPS fly the hold at the arc's end, saying the box will warn her if she drifts out of the holding airspace. What do you teach?
options: The map is fine as the primary guide on the arc, but she must hand-fly the hold, since only GPS holds can leave the airspace
Both are fine with WAAS, because a WAAS receiver adds the holding airspace limits to its alerts and to its moving map
The map is a cross-check, not the primary source, and an RNAV system cannot warn her of leaving the holding airspace
The hold is fine, but on the arc she should check the map against the DME groundspeed, which is accurate on an arc
questions.why: AFMs prohibit using the moving map as the primary data source [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]], so the arc is flown on the DME and the needles with the map as a cross-check. RNAV systems cannot alert the pilot to excursions outside holding protected airspace, because its dimensions are not in the navigation database [[33:390|AIM 5-3-8j7(b)]]; nothing in the AIM gives WAAS that ability. DME groundspeed is accurate only when tracking directly to or from the station [[23:260|IFH 9-17]], so it is not accurate on an arc. Hand-flying is no cure either: departing from the recommended entries with excess speed at the fix can take any airplane outside the protected airspace [[33:386|AIM 5-3-8j3]].

questions.q: Your learner tracks the 180 radial inbound to a VOR, where she will hold south on that radial. The CDI drifts left; she turns 20° left, the needle centers, and she turns back to 360°. It drifts left again. What do you teach for the track and for the hold?
options: Re-center the needle with the OBS each time it drifts; in the hold, use that same correction outbound, the other way
Halve it to 10° left and refine; in the hold, keep the same left correction outbound, since the wind is unchanged
Hold the 20° left until the VOR; in the hold, fly the outbound leg with no correction and fix the wind by timing
Halve it to 10° left and refine; in the hold, triple the final inbound correction, the other way, on the outbound leg
questions.why: When a 20° correction brings the needle back to center, the IFH has the pilot cut it in half, not remove it, then make smaller corrections [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. Re-centering the needle with the OBS and flying the new course is homing, which follows a circuitous route [[23:257|IFH 9-14]], and chasing the CDI with no bracketing is a listed VOR error [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. The correction that holds the needle is her inbound drift correction. Outbound she flies the reciprocal, and the AIM triples the correction the other way: 8° left inbound means 24° right outbound [[33:391|AIM 5-3-8j8(c)]]. The IFH expects drift corrections on both legs plus a time allowance on the outbound leg, so timing alone does not fix the wind [[23:301|IFH 10-10]].

questions.q: Your learner's GPS route uses fly-by waypoints and ends at a holding fix, and she will let the GPS fly the hold. She says turn anticipation is normal, so an early turn at the holding fix is fine too. What do you teach?
options: She is right: turn anticipation is allowed for in all airspace, so the hold's protected area includes the early turn
Holds assume flying over the fix on entry, so an early turn can leave the airspace; slow early and use 25° of bank
She is right for a direct entry only, since only teardrop and parallel entries assume flying over the fix first
The early turn is fine if she limits the bank to 15°, which keeps the turn inside the hold's protected airspace
questions.why: Fly-by waypoints let the airplane turn before the waypoint, and that turn anticipation is compensated for in the airspace and terrain clearances; a holding waypoint, though, is always designed as a fly-over waypoint in the database [[33:99|AIM 1-1-17]]. Holding protected airspace assumes the airplane flies over the fix on initial entry, and an RNAV fly-by turn there, even during a direct entry from the holding side, can take it beyond the protected airspace [[33:388|AIM 5-3-8j7(a)(2)]]. Slowing to the maximum holding speed at least 3 minutes before the fix and using the recommended 25° bank reduce that risk [[33:391|AIM 5-3-8j8(e)]]. A shallower bank widens and lengthens the track [[33:389|AIM 5-3-8j7(a)(3)]], so 15° makes it worse.

questions.q: Cleared for a VOR approach, your learner joins the final approach course from a DME arc whose segment is marked NoPT. A hold in lieu of procedure turn is charted at the fix where the arc ends. She plans one circuit of it to get settled. What do you teach?
options: Fine: a charted hold in lieu of procedure turn is required, so one circuit is expected whichever way she arrives
Not as planned: with NoPT on her route she flies straight in unless she tells ATC and is cleared for the hold
Fine, as long as she stays at or below the maximum holding speed and keeps within the charted leg length
Fine, if she uses the entry that fits her heading and tells ATC once the circuit is done and she is inbound
questions.why: When a holding pattern replaces a procedure turn it must be followed, except when radar vectoring is provided or NoPT is shown on the approach course; where the procedure specifies NoPT, no pilot may make a procedure turn unless she advises ATC when the approach clearance is received and is cleared for it [[33:428|AIM 5-4-9b]]. The IPH agrees: a DME arc is an approach segment, the hold in lieu of procedure turn is not permitted when No PT is depicted on the segment being flown, and a pilot who wants it must first get an amended clearance [[29:183|IPH 4-43]]. The speed and leg limits are real for a hold in lieu of procedure turn [[33:428|AIM 5-4-9a5]], but they don't authorize it, and telling ATC afterward is too late.

questions.q: Your learner tracks outbound on the 045 radial of a VOR/DME. ATC says: "Hold southwest of the 20 DME fix on the 045 radial, 4-mile legs." Using FIG 5-3-6 as the model, where is the fix, and where does each outbound leg end?
options: The fix is 20 DME on the 045 radial, and each outbound leg ends when the DME reads 24
The fix is 20 DME on the 045 radial, and each outbound leg ends 1 minute after abeam
The fix is 16 DME on the 045 radial, and each outbound leg ends when the DME reads 20
The fix is 20 DME on the 045 radial, and each outbound leg ends when the DME reads 16
questions.why: DME holding uses the same entry and holding procedures with distances in place of time; the end of the outbound leg is set by the DME readout, and on conventional holds both ends are measured from the DME station [[33:387|AIM 5-3-8j5]]. Holding southwest of a fix that is northeast of the station puts the pattern on the station side, so the inbound course runs away from the NAVAID. As in FIG 5-3-6, where a 28 NM fix with 8 NM legs gives 20 DME, the outbound end is the fix distance minus the leg length: 20 - 4 = 16 [[33:387|AIM 5-3-8j5]]. Adding the legs (24) is the toward-the-NAVAID case, and a leg in minutes is given only on request or when the controller thinks it necessary [[33:382|AIM 5-3-8i]].

questions.q: Your learner flies the 10 DME arc of a VOR clockwise from the east and will reach the 10 DME fix on the 180 radial heading about 270°. ATC says: "Hold south of the 10 DME fix on the 180 radial, 5-mile legs." Using FIG 5-3-4, which entry does she fly, and where do the outbound legs end?
options: A teardrop entry, with every outbound leg ending when the DME reads 15
A direct entry, with each outbound leg ending when the DME reads 15
A parallel entry, with each outbound leg ending when the DME reads 15
A parallel entry, with each outbound leg ending when the DME reads 5
questions.why: No turn direction was given, so she flies right turns [[29:111|IPH 2-51]]. The inbound course is 360° toward the VOR and the outbound course 180°. The entry is chosen from the heading on arrival at the fix [[33:391|AIM 5-3-8j8(d)]]: on 270° the outbound course is 90° to her left, inside the 110° parallel sector of FIG 5-3-4, not the 70° teardrop sector on the other side [[33:386|AIM 5-3-8j3]]. With the inbound course toward the NAVAID, the outbound end is the fix distance plus the leg length, 10 + 5 = 15 [[33:387|AIM 5-3-8j5]]; 5 DME would be the away-from-the-NAVAID case.

questions.q: Your learner is holding at an en route VOR with an EFC of 1530. The VOR is not a fix where an approach begins; her approach starts at an IAF on a DME arc 20 miles away. At 1510 her radios fail in IMC. Under 14 CFR 91.185, what does she do?
options: Hold until 1530, fly to the IAF, and start the approach as close as possible to her ETA
Leave the hold now and fly to the IAF, since a radio failure cancels the EFC and the hold
Hold until her ETA, then fly to the IAF and start the arc as soon as she arrives there
Hold until 1530, fly to the IAF, and start the approach at once, since the EFC was its start
questions.why: If the clearance limit is not a fix from which an approach begins, the pilot leaves it at the EFC, proceeds to a fix from which an approach begins, and starts descent or descent and approach as close as possible to the ETA calculated from the filed or amended estimated time en route [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)]]. Starting the approach as close as possible to the EFC is the rule only when the holding fix is where the approach begins [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)]], and nothing in the rule cancels the EFC. The IPH notes that the EFC is what lets a pilot with lost radios leave the holding fix at a definite time [[29:111|IPH 2-51]].

questions.q: Your learner's ILS has a missed approach that ends in a hold at an NDB, and the chart notes "ADF required." Her airplane has no ADF but has a TSO-C146 GPS with a current database. What do you teach?
options: She can't fly it: an "ADF required" note can be met only by a working ADF in the airplane
She may hold on the GPS at any waypoint near the NDB, letting the receiver keep sequencing
She may hold on the GPS: the NDB is the active waypoint, flown in a nonsequencing mode
She may use the GPS only if ATC approves first, as substitution is not allowed on a missed approach
questions.why: A suitable RNAV system, which includes TSO-C146 equipment authorized for IFR en route and terminal operations, may substitute when the airplane has no ADF, and may be used to hold over an NDB [[33:116|AIM 1-2-3a]] [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3b]] [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3c]]. These allowances apply even when a facility is identified as required on a procedure, for example "ADF required" [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3c]]. The IFH steps for a GPS hold over an NDB: check integrity, select the charted NDB from the database as the active waypoint (if it is not in the database, its use is not authorized), and select a nonsequencing mode such as HOLD or OBS with the course [[23:271|IFH 9-28]]. The AIM says only that a pilot substituting for an out-of-service NAVAID may need to advise ATC [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]], and it lists holding over an NDB among the uses with no missed approach exception.

questions.q: Your learner reaches a VOR that is the IAF, with a hold in lieu of procedure turn and no NoPT route from her direction. After the entry, on the outbound leg at the holding altitude, she is cleared for the approach. When may she descend to the FAF altitude, and must she fly more circuits?
options: Right away on the outbound leg, since she is cleared; no more circuits are needed
Once she turns back inbound, before she is on course; one more circuit is required
Only when established on the inbound course; one full circuit after entry is required
Only when she is established on the inbound course; ATC expects no further circuits
questions.why: When a holding pattern replaces a procedure turn, descent from the minimum holding altitude to the FAF altitude may not begin until the airplane is established on the inbound course [[33:428|AIM 5-4-9b3]]. If she is cleared for the approach before returning to the holding fix and is at the prescribed altitude, more circuits are neither necessary nor expected; a pilot who wants one to lose altitude or get better established tells ATC on receiving the approach clearance [[33:428|AIM 5-4-9a5]]. The approach clearance does not allow a descent on the outbound leg, and turning toward the course is not being established on it.

questions.q: After weeks of right-turn holds, your learner intercepts the holding radial well and is cleared to hold with left turns. At the fix she turns right, then says she knew the clearance said left. How does the AIH classify this, and what do you do?
options: A slip, from doing a routine in a slightly different way; point it out and ask her why it happened
A mistake, an error of thought about left turns; reteach the entry sectors before she flies again
A slip, caused by gaps in her knowledge; stop holding practice and reteach the whole holding chapter
A mistake, caused by time pressure; take the controls at once and fly the rest of the hold for her
questions.why: A slip is an error of action: planning one thing and doing another, and one form happens when a person is asked to perform a routine procedure in a slightly different way, as in the AIH's runway 30 and runway 12 example. A mistake is an error of thought, often from gaps or misconceptions in understanding, and time pressure is a source of slips [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]. She knew the clearance, so this is a slip. The AIH has the instructor point out errors when they occur and ask the learner to explain why they occurred [[25:86|AIH 3-35]], and correcting errors does not mean taking over at once: safety permitting, let the learner find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Left-turn holds use the same entries, oriented to the 70° line on the holding side [[33:386|AIM 5-3-8j3(e)]].

questions.q: With GPS lateral guidance, your learner flies toward a VOR to hold north on the 360 radial, standard turns. In a strong west wind she is heading 350° on a track of 005°. She calls a teardrop entry; the GPS sets up a parallel. What do you teach?
options: The GPS has failed, since every receiver picks the entry from heading; she flies the teardrop by hand
Both are reasonable: the AIM uses heading, many GPS units use track, and she may let the GPS pick
She is wrong: the AIM bases the entry on track over the ground, so the parallel is the only right one
Neither is right: this close to a sector line, the AIM calls for a direct entry to stay protected
questions.why: The AIM has the pilot determine the entry from the heading on arrival at the fix, with ±5° counted as within good operating limits, and when RNAV lateral guidance is used for holding it is permissible to let the system compute the entry [[33:391|AIM 5-3-8j8(d)]]. Many RNAV systems use ground track instead of heading to select the entry, which can give an unexpected entry when the wind causes a large drift angle [[33:388|AIM 5-3-8j7(a)(1)]]. Here the outbound course, 360°, is 10° right of her heading, in the teardrop sector, but 5° left of her track, in the parallel sector [[33:386|AIM 5-3-8j3]]. Nothing in the AIM calls for a direct entry near a sector line. Application: brief the GPS's likely entry before a windy hold.
